name: Thomas theorem
statement: If men define situations as real, they are real in their consequences: what a situation means to those in it governs what they do.
meaning: Action follows the meaning a situation carries for the person in it, and the consequences of that action are real whatever the situation was in objective terms. The sentence is the last line of a methodological argument rather than a general law. It closes Chapter XIII of The Child in America, The Methodology of Behavior Study, which defends the case history, the life record and the psychoanalytic confession against the objection, which the Thomases attribute to the school of behaviourism, that introspective records have no objectivity or validity. Their answer is that a subject's account reveals the situation that conditioned the behaviour, and that this holds even for a record as far from objective reality as a delusion of persecution. Merton kept the theorem separate from the self-fulfilling prophecy, and the difference is one clause. The prophecy needs the opening definition to be false. The theorem does not.

origin.who: W. I. Thomas and Dorothy Swaine Thomas
origin.where: The Child in America: Behavior Problems and Programs (New York: Alfred A. Knopf), page 572
origin.note: The sentence closes a paragraph on the evidential value of subjective records, in a chapter on research method. Its illustration is an inmate of Dannemora prison who had killed several people who talked to themselves in the street, because he read insults off the movement of their lips and behaved as if that were true. The eponym is Merton's. He wrote of 'W. I. Thomas' sociological theorem' on pages 331 to 332 of a 1938 paper in Philosophy of Science, and used 'the Thomas theorem' in his 1948 paper on the self-fulfilling prophecy.

evidence: There is no study behind the theorem. It is one sentence, supported by one anecdote, in a chapter about research method. The anecdote is the refusal of the warden of Dannemora prison to send an inmate out under a court order, and the book does not say where the Thomases got it. Merton's first use of the eponym, in 1938, called the theorem repeatedly verified and cited nothing for it. His 1948 use added no data either: his illustration is a fictional bank called the Last National, and his point is that the same thought had been set down before Thomas by Bossuet, Mandeville, Marx, Freud and Sumner, whose agreement he takes as reason to attend to it. In 1995 he added Epictetus and Schopenhauer, and noted that George Herbert Mead had told his Chicago classes that 'If a thing is not recognized as true, then it does not function as true in the community', a formulation published in 1936 which then sank. What has been measured is the sentence's circulation. Merton reports that none of the reviews of The Child in America in the American Journal of Sociology, Social Forces or Sociology and Social Research took any notice of the theorem. Kimball Young made it a chapter epigraph in his Social Psychology in 1930 and in Social Attitudes in 1931, both times without a source reference, and Merton calls those epigraphs an early conduit for its spread. R. S. Smith surveyed well over 100 introductory sociology textbooks and found 40 that quoted or paraphrased the theorem, of which one cited the book and page it came from. Those figures are Merton quoting the conference paper Smith gave in 1993, not the article Smith published in 1995. By Merton's count W. I. Thomas put the sentence in print three times in his career: the 1928 book, an essay in a 1931 Brookings Institution symposium, and Blumer's 1939 appraisal of The Polish Peasant. He never developed it.

replication.headline: No replication or direct empirical test of the theorem was located. The nearest experimental evidence belongs to the self-fulfilling prophecy, which is a narrower claim and has its own entry.
replication.detail: The theorem is not an experimental prediction. It names no population, no manipulation and no outcome, and Merton calls the sentence in its original setting an 'essentially methodological observation'. There is nothing in it that a repetition could confirm or overturn in the way an effect size can. The literature that does run experiments is the expectancy work, which sits in this atlas under self-fulfilling prophecy at entry 44 and the Pygmalion effect at entry 9. Those studies test something stronger and more specific: that a false expectation held by one person changes the behaviour of another, measurably, without either party knowing. Results there are mixed, and they are not evidence for or against the Thomases' sentence. The mirror case, the self-defeating prophecy at entry 218, is no more a test of the theorem than the expectancy work is. A reader who wants numbers should go to those entries and should not treat a finding about teacher expectations as a test of the theorem.

limits: Searches for a replication or a direct empirical test were re-run on 21 September 2026 against Crossref's bibliographic index, pairing the theorem and its opening words with 'replication', 'empirical test' and 'experiment'. They returned dictionary entries, commentary and citation studies, and nothing that put the proposition at risk. OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar answered their search endpoints with a rate limit that day, so those two indexes were not searched. The only counting exercise located is Smith's textbook survey, which measures how the sentence is cited rather than whether it holds. Merton quotes that survey from a paper Smith read to the Eastern Sociological Society in 1993, and his reference list marks the American Sociologist version as in press, so the figures here are one remove from Smith and need not be the ones his article prints. Smith's papers of 1995 and 1999 are still shut. Springer answers for both and posts the 1995 abstract and the whole of the 1999 conclusion, which were read, behind a subscription offer rather than a refusal, and Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar both record no open copy. Merton's 1938 paper was opened in a scan of the July 1938 issue at the Internet Archive, and the eponym sits on pages 331 to 332. His 1995 running text gives that page as 333 twice, the letter he reprints in the same article gives 331 to 332, and the letter is right. That 1995 article was read as a scan in Eugene Garfield's Merton collection at the University of Pennsylvania, with optical character recognition errors throughout. Dorothy Swaine Thomas's letter of 10 September 1973 survives only as Merton reproduced it there, and he prints no reply from her to the claims he later built on it.
misreadings: The theorem is routinely credited to W. I. Thomas alone. Merton did that first and defended it for the rest of his life, on the strength of a letter Dorothy Swaine Thomas wrote him on 10 September 1973, saying that Thomas had employed her after the Rockefeller group told him to get himself a statistician, that 'The statistical portions were mine' and that 'The concept of "defining the situation" was strictly W.I.'s.' Smith's answer is that the sentence sits in a co-authored book, in a chapter no note assigns to either author, so either could have written it and both names belong on it unless there is compelling evidence otherwise. In 1999 he put it as the evidence for W. I. Thomas's sole authorship being far from conclusive. Smith also found that most textbooks name W. I. Thomas alone, that the few citing the book often drop its second author, and that her name does not begin to appear in the books he surveyed until the mid-1970s. Merton reports that the same point had reached him five years before Smith's survey, in a 1988 letter from a social scientist he leaves anonymous. The wording drifts as well. Willard Waller quoted it in 1938 as 'If people define things as real, they are real in their consequences', altering two words, and Merton reads the second change as evidence that the first was a slip rather than a de-gendering. Howard P. Becker located it on page 79 of the one-volume Polish Peasant, where Merton reports it is not to be found, and concluded that it was 'probably Znaniecki's'. The theorem is also not the self-fulfilling prophecy, which requires the first definition to be wrong. Merton's own warning is against the strong reading, in which only definitions of the situation are held to determine action and its consequences, and which converts the theorem into the maxim that if men do not define situations as real, they are not real in their consequences.

sources.text: Thomas, W. I., & Thomas, D. S. (1928). The Child in America: Behavior Problems and Programs. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. Read as a scan of the first edition. The theorem and its Dannemora illustration are on page 572, in Chapter XIII, The Methodology of Behavior Study; the preface is signed by both authors and the book nowhere divides the chapters between them.

Merton, R. K. (1995). The Thomas Theorem and the Matthew Effect. Social Forces, 74(2), 379-424. Read as a scanned copy in Eugene Garfield's Merton collection; source for the authorship correspondence, the diffusion history and the quotations from Smith's 1993 conference paper.

Merton, R. K. (1948). The Self-Fulfilling Prophecy. The Antioch Review, 8(2), 193-210. Read from a scan of the JSTOR original; source for the 1948 use of the eponym, the Last National Bank illustration and the list of anticipations.

Merton, R. K. (1938). Science and the Social Order. Philosophy of Science, 5(3), 321-337. Read in the Internet Archive's scan of the July 1938 issue; source for the first use of the eponym, which runs across pages 331 and 332 and reads 'W. I. Thomas' sociological theorem'.

Smith, R. S. (1995). Giving credit where credit is due: Dorothy Swaine Thomas and the 'Thomas Theorem'. The American Sociologist, 26(4), 9-28. Full text behind a subscription; the publisher's posted abstract was read, and is the source for the finding that her name first appears in the surveyed textbooks in the mid-1970s.

Smith, R. S. (1999). Contested memory: Notes on Robert K. Merton's 'The Thomas Theorem and the Matthew Effect'. The American Sociologist, 30(2), 62-77. Full text behind a subscription; the publisher posts the article's conclusion in full, and that is the source for Smith's own statement of his position.
